why: The repository ships the complete algorithm (aif_alg.py, self-contained with only numpy/random imports), the experiment notebook that produces Table I, and the exact Diabetes data (data/diabetes.csv) used in the claims. No weights or external downloads are needed, and the procedure is pure CPU on 768 rows, so the authors' entrypoint should run as-is with at most a numpy/scipy/jupyter install.
missing_artifacts: requirements.txt / pinned environment (not provided, but only numpy, scipy, pandas, jupyter are implied)
fixed random seeds for the reported Table I numbers (likely set in the notebook, to be confirmed on inspection)
blockers_seen: No dependency manifest; environment must be inferred (numpy/scipy/pandas/jupyter)
experiments.ipynb is ~828 KB (carries large embedded outputs), which can be slow to load but does not block execution
No GPU on this machine, but the workload is CPU-only so this is not a blocker

feasibility.est_runtime_on_this_machine: Under 5 minutes for the match target (C1): one EIF forest + one AIF(A3) forest (500 trees, subsample 128, 768 rows) and a t-test. Full Table I (EIF + A3/A4/A5 across ~8 features) is around 10-15 minutes including installs.
feasibility.scale_down_plan: None needed. If the notebook turns out to run many extra unrelated experiments, restrict execution to the Diabetes Table I cells (EIF vs A3/A4/A5); this does not change the reported numbers.

compute.basis: 500-tree isolation forests on 768x8 tabular data with subsample 128 is a sub-second-to-few-second fit per forest, so the Table I protocol (a handful of forests plus t-tests) is ~10-15 min of command time, dominated by environment install and notebook startup.
